stories.headline: Update: Trump Accuses Iran of Killing Americans and Protesters as Qatar Prepares Regional Defense Agreement
stories.summary:
President Donald Trump sharply criticized Iran's government during remarks in Kansas on Monday. He accused the regime of killing Americans with roadside bombs and of hanging protesters from cranes. Fox News live coverage also reported that Qatar is preparing to announce a regional defense agreement, and that Iran has issued a warning to the United States.

Trump said Tehran had sought assurances about its own treatment. "They wanted me to guarantee that we won't kill them like we killed the others," he said, adding that Iran had "killed a lot of Americans with their roadside bombs over the years." He referred to the 2020 U.S. drone strike that killed Iranian Gen. Qassem Soleimani during his first term. He also claimed that Iranian authorities had killed at least 75,000 protesters in the last eight months, a figure that was stated in his remarks and was not independently verified in the reporting provided.

The remarks come as the Middle East conflict continues to draw in regional actors and as Washington debates how the war should end. Vice President JD Vance has said the U.S. has "decisively won" the war in some ways, while Trump has tied Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's re-election to the question of whether the U.S. must "finish the job" against Iran. Critics of the administration question the strategy and the lack of a clear endpoint, while supporters say a hard line is needed to prevent Iran from obtaining nuclear weapons.

The Qatar defense agreement, if announced, would add a new element to the regional security picture. Further details of the pact and any Iranian response are expected in coming days.

stories.headline: Update: Zelensky and US Envoys to Hold Oslo Talks as Rubio Denies Withholding Intelligence
stories.summary:
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky and U.S. special envoy Steve Witkoff are due to meet in Oslo, Norway, as relations between Kyiv and Washington deteriorate. Jared Kushner is to take part by video link. Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Store said Zelensky asked Norway and Finland to organize the meeting with the U.S. and European allies "at a critical time for Ukraine." Finnish President Alexander Stubb also met Zelensky ahead of the talks.

Secretary of State Marco Rubio, who is visiting India, called accusations that Ukrainians were dying because the U.S. was withholding intelligence "scandalous" and "outrageous." The claims came from Zelensky's military technical adviser, Serhii "Flash" Beskrestnov, who told the BBC that unreliable U.S. warnings were costing lives. Rubio acknowledged that Patriot interceptor missiles may not yet have arrived in Ukraine but said nothing had been denied to Kyiv intentionally. Zelensky said he had a "constructive discussion" with Rubio about early warnings, interceptors and Starlink service.

Tensions have grown in recent weeks. Trump has said it is time for Ukraine to get a new president and for "somebody else to negotiate on behalf of Ukraine." Last week a bipartisan group of senators called for an urgent investigation into disruptions to Starlink in Ukraine. Trump also recently announced, after a call with Vladimir Putin, that Russia would supply more than 300,000 tons of diesel and that U.S. sanctions on Russian diesel exports would end, a move that drew criticism including from some Republicans.

Store said the aim of the talks is to steer relations toward "a more constructive path" and a lasting, just peace. It is unclear whether Witkoff will travel on to Russia, though Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said he hopes a meeting can be organized soon.

stories.headline: Update: Marseille Braces for More Unrest After Weekend of Looting and Violence
stories.summary:
Marseille is preparing for further unrest after Saturday's protests turned into widespread disorder in France's second city. Local business leaders say more than 500 premises were damaged, most of them looted, including shops along La Canebiere, Rue Paradis and the Centre Bourse shopping centre, as well as malls in the city's north.

A police union official described the weekend as "apocalyptic." Arnaud Blaise of the UN1TE union said, "It was a war," calling the violence unprecedented. In Marseille, 118 officers were injured, more than a tenth of the national total, and 101 arrests have been made, a quarter of them children. Blaise attributed the chaos to far-left agitators and said young people from deprived northern suburbs exploited it to steal; this characterization is his own and was not independently established.

On Monday authorities banned demonstrations and gatherings for eight hours, and the city was largely calm, with police far more visible than protesters. An overnight curfew for minors will take effect in parts of the city from Tuesday evening. A suspect has also been arrested after the historic town hall in Limoges was set alight, according to French media.

Some demonstrators defended the protests' aims while condemning the looting. One 18-year-old student described the march's solidarity as "beautiful" and the later disorder as "terrifying." The government faces mounting political pressure after the nationwide riots, in which about 1,800 people were arrested.

stories.headline: Michigan Senate Race Enters Final Two Weeks as Rogers Targets El-Sayed's Support Among Black and Jewish Voters
stories.summary:
Republican Senate nominee Mike Rogers said at a Fox News town hall Monday night that Democratic nominee Abdul El-Sayed is vulnerable among two traditionally Democratic blocs, Black and Jewish voters. The Michigan contest is one of the nation's most closely watched Senate races, with Election Day on Nov. 3.

Rogers said Black pastors and neighborhood leaders in Detroit are "looking for a change," and pointed to El-Sayed's past remark that Barack Obama was "not the right choice" to advance a progressive agenda. Obama is scheduled to campaign with El-Sayed in Detroit on Oct. 24 and has released a video backing him. Rogers also said that if half of Michigan's roughly 70,000 Jewish Democrats voted for him, it would bring about 35,000 votes and change the race's dynamic.

Rogers cited El-Sayed's criticism of Israel. In a recent debate, El-Sayed declined to say whether he considers Iran or Israel the greater threat, saying both "have proven dangerous in their own way." Republican gubernatorial nominee John James and Rep. Lisa McClain also appeared, seeking to tie Michigan Democrats to government spending and the party's progressive wing.

El-Sayed's campaign and Democrats have argued that he represents a new generation focused on affordability and working-class concerns, and Obama's involvement is intended to consolidate the party's base. The race is part of a broader midterm landscape in which President Trump's approval has fallen to record lows, giving Democrats an edge in some polling.

stories.headline: Albanian Protesters Clash With Police for Seventh Day in Bid to Oust Prime Minister Rama
stories.summary:
Protesters in Albania fought with riot police on Monday for the seventh consecutive day. The demonstrators, many of them high school and university students, are demanding the resignation of Prime Minister Edi Rama. Their grievances include poor university conditions and anger over corruption. Official figures said 295 people had been injured before Monday's violence, 186 of them police officers.

A police station and government buildings in Tirana have been attacked during the unrest. Rama, brandishing a rock thrown at police on Sunday, told police chiefs that "the moment the state negotiates with this, the state has fallen." He said the protesters included young people "radicalised by dark forces in Europe and the US" and claimed Albania had become the target of a "well co-ordinated attack."

A BBC correspondent in Tirana's Rinia Park watched protesters pry up cobblestones to use as projectiles. Police advanced with an armoured truck firing water cannon and tear gas, and riot squads chased the largely student crowd through the park. Human rights lawyer Gentian Sejrani, who is providing legal support to more than 100 detainees, said police actions were often chaotic and that officers rarely present evidence in court. He said those who actually throw objects are seldom caught.

The movement has no formal leadership, and activists coordinate informally to arrange first aid, legal help and protest locations. Police, for their part, appear angered by the injuries to their colleagues. The standoff shows no sign of easing, and the government has so far rejected negotiation.

stories.headline: Japanese Spacecraft Launches Toward Mars' Moon Phobos to Retrieve Sample
stories.summary:
A Japanese-led spacecraft launched Tuesday on a mission to Phobos, one of Mars' two moons, where it will attempt to collect surface material and return it to Earth. If successful, it would be the first sample ever returned from Mars or its moons. The Mars Moons Exploration (MMX) mission is led by the Japanese space agency JAXA and is scheduled to arrive at Phobos in August 2027.

The spacecraft will first study the smaller moon Deimos as it approaches, then focus on Phobos, which is about 20 km across. It plans to deploy a small rover to scout a landing site, a difficult task because Phobos has very little gravity while sitting next to Mars' much stronger gravitational pull. The main craft will then touch down, use a robotic arm and two samplers to collect about 10 grams of dust, and send it back in a capsule landing in the Woomera desert of South Australia in 2031.

Scientists hope the sample will resolve how Mars' moons formed. One hypothesis holds that a space rock struck Mars early in its history and the moons formed from the debris. The other holds that they are asteroids from the outer Solar System captured by Mars' gravity. Sara Russell of the Natural History Museum said the two ideas would produce very distinct chemistry and mineral results, so the answer should be quickly apparent. Researchers say even a tiny sample can support extensive study of individual grains.

stories.headline: Rep. Garcia Says ICE Officers Broke U.S. Citizen's Arm in Long Beach
stories.summary:
Rep. Robert Garcia (D-Calif.) said Immigration and Customs Enforcement officers broke the arm of a U.S. citizen in North Long Beach over the weekend. "ICE agents brutally attacked and broke the arm of a North Long Beach resident and U.S. citizen. The videos are horrific and should concern not just our community but the country," Garcia said.

Police in Long Beach said ICE called them for backup and that officers arriving at the scene found a man who was bleeding and handcuffed. The details of what led to the confrontation and the extent of the man's injuries were not fully laid out in the available reporting, and it was not clear whether DHS had responded to the allegation.

The episode adds to an ongoing national debate over immigration enforcement tactics. Democrats and immigrant advocacy groups have repeatedly criticized aggressive ICE operations and cited cases involving citizens. Supporters of the enforcement push, including the administration, generally argue that officers face resistance and that agents act within the law. Further information from DHS, Long Beach police and the man's representatives is expected.

stories.headline: Air Force Sergeant Dies After Fall During Pregame Ceremony at Alamodome
stories.summary:
A U.S. Air Force member died after falling while abseiling from the ceiling of San Antonio's Alamodome before a college football game on Saturday. Footage showed the serviceman plummet feet first to the turf at midfield during a ceremony ahead of the game between the University of Texas at San Antonio and the Naval Academy. The dome's ceiling is about 170 feet high.

The military identified him as Tech. Sgt. Ian Patterson, a Tactical Air Control Party instructor at Joint Base San Antonio and a member of the 57th Wing. He died in hospital. Patterson, of Fort Stewart, Georgia, had served 15 years and was named the Air Force Special Warfare Enlisted Instructor of the Year at the headquarters level in 2022.

The incident is under investigation. The game went ahead as planned, and the American Conference said the decision to continue was made before his death was confirmed. Brig. Gen. Scott Mills said the tragedy was "felt deeply across the 57th Wing," and UTSA president Taylor Eighmy offered condolences to Patterson's family and fellow airmen.
